client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of a task and just completely lose track of what I was doing, or I'll find myself staring at nothing for long stretches of time. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds really heavy — losing your grandmother and then trying to function normally at work while grieving is an enormous ask of yourself. Your skepticism about talking makes complete sense too, because you're right that nothing will change that loss, and I want to honor that truth rather than gloss over it. I'm curious though — even if talking can't bring her back, is there anything you're hoping might feel even slightly different for you, even in a small way?

client: I guess... maybe I just want to stop feeling like I'm going to fall apart every time someone at work asks me how I'm doing. Like I have to hold it together constantly and pretend everything's fine, and it's exhausting. I don't know if that's something talking can actually fix, but that's the only thing I can think of that might feel different.
therapist: That goal makes so much sense — the constant effort of holding yourself together while quietly grieving underneath is genuinely exhausting, and it's not a small thing to want relief from that. What you're describing, that gap between what you're feeling inside and what you're showing the world, is something we can actually work with together. I'm wondering, when someone asks how you're doing and you feel that pressure to hold it together, what's the thought that goes through your mind in that moment?

client: When someone asks how I'm doing, the first thing that pops into my head is something like "don't make this weird" or "they don't actually want to know." It's almost automatic, like a reflex, and before I even have time to think I've already said "I'm fine, just tired" or something like that. I guess I worry that if I said anything real, it would either burden them or they'd look at me differently, and I can't afford to lose the few connections I have.
therapist: Those automatic thoughts — "don't make this weird" and "they don't actually want to know" — are doing a lot of protective work for you, even if they're also quietly isolating you at a time when connection might matter most. It's really understandable that you'd want to guard the relationships you have, especially when you're already feeling so vulnerable. I'm curious — is there anyone in your life where you've tested that fear, even a little, and let them see even a glimpse of how you're really doing?

client: I mean... maybe my sister, a little bit. A few weeks ago I kind of hinted that I'd been having a rough time, and she didn't run away or change the subject, she actually asked a follow-up question. But then I kind of deflected and made a joke, because I got scared it was going to become this whole thing and I'd end up feeling like a burden to her.
therapist: What you just described with your sister is actually really significant — she didn't pull away, she leaned in, and that's real evidence that pushes back against the thought that opening up will burden people or make things weird. It sounds like the fear kicked in right at the moment of possibility, which is such a human and understandable response when you're feeling this fragile. I'm wondering, what do you think would have happened if, instead of deflecting with the joke, you'd let her ask that follow-up question?

client: Honestly, I think part of me knows she would have just... listened. Like, she probably wouldn't have run away or thought I was being dramatic. But there's this other part that's convinced if I actually said out loud how lonely I've been feeling, it would become too real, and then I'd have to sit with the fact that I've been struggling this much without telling anyone — and that feels almost more shameful than the loneliness itself.
therapist: What you just named takes a lot of courage to say — that the shame of having struggled silently might feel heavier than the struggle itself is such an honest and painful insight. It's worth gently noticing though, that keeping it hidden hasn't protected you from the loneliness, it's just meant you've been carrying it completely alone. I'm curious — where do you think that sense of shame about needing support comes from for you?

client: Yeah, I think you're right that hiding it hasn't actually made the loneliness go away, it's just... made it quieter in a way that felt safer. I guess the shame comes from growing up in a family where you just didn't talk about that stuff, like needing help was the same as being weak or a burden to everyone else. My parents were dealing with their own things and I learned pretty early that I was supposed to just handle it myself.
therapist: What you just shared is really important — you learned a survival rule very early that kept you safe in your family, but it sounds like that rule has followed you into adulthood and is now costing you connection when you need it most. The belief that needing help equals being weak or a burden isn't a truth about you, it's something you were taught, and those are very different things. I'm wondering, if your sister came to you struggling and needed to lean on you, would you see her as weak or a burden?

client: I mean... no, of course I wouldn't see her that way. I'd want her to come to me, actually. But it feels different when it's me being the one who needs something — like the rules just don't apply the same way, and I can't quite explain why that is.
therapist: You just caught something really important — you can clearly extend compassion to your sister without hesitation, but when it's you who needs something, a completely different and harsher set of rules kicks in. That double standard is so common, and it usually traces right back to what you learned early on, that *your* needs were the ones that had to be managed or hidden. I'm curious, what do you think it would mean about you if you actually allowed yourself the same care you'd so readily give to her?

client: I think it would mean I was... weak, or self-indulgent maybe. Like if I start treating my own needs as valid, I'm somehow admitting that I've been struggling all along, and that feels really exposing. I guess part of me worries that if I open that door, I won't be able to close it again — like everything I've been holding together will just fall apart.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just said — the fear that letting yourself be human and struggling might mean everything unravels. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if allowing things to "fall apart" a little isn't the opposite of holding it together, but actually part of how grief is supposed to move through you, rather than being held in place by sheer effort? I'm wondering, when you imagine that door opening and someone like your sister on the other side of it, does it feel quite as terrifying as when you imagine facing it alone?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, when I picture my sister being there... it does feel a little less like I'm standing at the edge of something I can't come back from. But then I catch myself thinking, what if I cry so hard I can't stop, or I say something that makes her worry about me even more than she already does? I don't want to become a burden to her on top of everything else she's dealing with since we lost Mom.
therapist: It's really meaningful that imagining your sister there makes it feel even a little less frightening — that's your own wisdom telling you something worth listening to. The fears about crying too hard or worrying her make complete sense, but I notice you're already taking care of her feelings even in this imagined moment, which is actually the opposite of what a burden does. I'm curious — you mentioned "since we lost Mom," and I want to make sure I'm understanding, are you and your sister both grieving right now, and is it possible she might actually need this connection with you just as much as you need it with her?

client: Yeah, we're both grieving. She lost Mom too, obviously, and I know that logically she probably does want to be close right now. But somehow knowing that doesn't make it easier to pick up the phone — if anything it almost makes it harder, because then I feel like I should be stronger for her, not falling apart myself.
therapist: There's something quietly painful in what you just described — you're both grieving the same loss, both probably longing for each other, and yet the belief that you need to be the strong one is keeping you at a distance from the very person who might understand most. I'm wondering if it's possible that your sister has her own version of this same thought, each of you waiting to reach out until you feel strong enough, which means you might both be sitting alone with it unnecessarily. What do you think would happen if you called her not to fall apart *at* her, but just to say "I've been missing you and I think we both need this"?
